concepts.definition: A continuous alimentary canal through which food passes from the oral cavity to the anus.
Organs that aid digestion through mechanical actions or secretions without carrying food through their interiors.
Mechanical and chemical breakdown of food into forms that can be absorbed.
Entry of food and drink into the GI tract through the mouth.
Physical crushing, shearing, mixing, or churning of food without breaking its chemical bonds.
Enzyme-mediated breakdown of large food molecules into smaller products.
Release of substances such as water, mucus, acid, buffers, enzymes, salts, and bile into the digestive tract.
Movement of nutrients, water, or ions across digestive epithelium into blood or lymph.
Removal of water from intestinal contents to concentrate fecal material.
Elimination of feces through the rectum and anus.
Breakdown of complex molecules into smaller molecules.
Synthesis of larger molecules from smaller precursors.
A moist mass of chewed food mixed with saliva before swallowing.
A semifluid mixture of partially digested food and gastric secretions.
Coordinated muscular mixing and propulsion of digestive contents.
Innermost GI wall layer; includes epithelium, lamina propria, and muscularis mucosae.
Connective-tissue GI layer containing larger vessels, lymphatics, and the submucosal nerve plexus.
Smooth-muscle layer producing propulsion and mixing, usually with inner circular and outer longitudinal layers.
Outer visceral peritoneal covering of many abdominal digestive organs.
Outer connective tissue layer anchoring an organ where a serosal covering is absent.
Enteric nerve network between muscularis externa layers that primarily regulates GI motility.
Enteric nerve network in the submucosa that helps regulate secretion and local blood flow.
Extensive network of neurons in the GI wall coordinating local digestive functions.
Sequential waves of muscular contraction that propel contents along the digestive tract.
Alternating intestinal contractions that mainly mix contents and increase contact with the mucosa.
Strong, relatively infrequent contractions that move colonic contents toward the rectum.
Slow mixing and movement within the haustra of the large intestine.
Serous membrane lining the abdominopelvic cavity and covering many organs.
Peritoneal layer lining the inside of the abdominal body wall.
Peritoneal layer covering the surfaces of many abdominal organs.
Double layer of peritoneum supporting organs and conveying vessels, nerves, and lymphatics.
Peritoneal apron extending from the greater curvature of the stomach over intestinal loops.
Peritoneal fold connecting the liver to the lesser curvature of the stomach and proximal duodenum.
Situated behind the parietal peritoneum rather than suspended within the peritoneal cavity.
Chewing food into smaller pieces using teeth, tongue, and jaw muscles.
Initial digestive chamber where food is tasted, chewed, lubricated, and partly digested.
Salivary enzyme that begins digestion of starch into smaller carbohydrates.
Fat-digesting enzyme released by glands associated with the tongue.
Salivary glycoproteins that lubricate food and help form a cohesive bolus.
Antimicrobial enzyme in saliva that can damage bacterial cell walls.
Salivary antibody contributing to immune protection of mucosal surfaces.
Large salivary gland near the ear that secretes watery, amylase-containing saliva.
Excretory duct conveying parotid saliva into the oral vestibule.
Salivary gland beneath the mandible contributing mixed serous and mucous secretion.
Main duct of the submandibular salivary gland opening in the floor of the mouth.
Salivary gland beneath the tongue that contributes especially mucous-rich secretion.
Multiple small ducts conveying secretion from the sublingual gland into the floor of the mouth.
Passage from the oral cavity into the oropharynx.
Midline projection hanging from the posterior soft palate.
Fold connecting the underside of the tongue to the floor of the mouth.
Fold connecting a lip to the adjacent gum tissue.
Superior surface of the tongue.
Anatomical term for the upper lip.
Anatomical term for the lower lip.
Highly mineralized outer material covering the tooth crown.
Mineralized tooth tissue underlying enamel and cementum and surrounding the pulp.
Mineralized covering of the tooth root to which the periodontal ligament attaches.
Central chamber of a tooth containing nerves, blood vessels, and connective tissue.
Opening near the root tip through which nerves and blood vessels enter a tooth.
Connective tissue anchoring tooth-root cementum to alveolar bone.
First set of human teeth, typically 20 in total.
Adult dentition, usually up to 32 teeth including third molars.
Swallowing process transferring a bolus from mouth through pharynx and esophagus to stomach.
Voluntary swallowing phase in which the tongue pushes the bolus toward the oropharynx.
Involuntary swallowing phase involving airway protection and passage into the esophagus.
Involuntary swallowing phase propelled by esophageal peristalsis.
Superior pharyngeal region serving as an air passage rather than a food route.
Middle pharyngeal region carrying both air and swallowed material.
Inferior pharyngeal region directing food toward the esophagus and air toward the larynx.
Elastic cartilage that helps protect the laryngeal inlet during swallowing, together with other airway-closure mechanisms.
Muscular region opening during swallowing and normally limiting air entry into the esophagus.
Distal esophageal high-pressure zone helping prevent reflux of stomach contents.
Brainstem region containing circuits important for coordinating reflex swallowing.
Opening in the diaphragm through which the esophagus passes.
Region of the stomach adjoining the esophageal opening.
Rounded superior part of the stomach, above and lateral to the cardia.
Largest central region of the stomach between fundus and pyloric region.
Distal stomach region leading to the duodenum.
Circular smooth muscle regulating delivery of chyme from the stomach into the duodenum.
Temporary folds in the stomach lining that flatten as it expands.
Additional innermost smooth muscle layer in the stomach assisting churning and mixing.
Secretory structures within gastric mucosa containing specialized epithelial and endocrine cells.
Gastric gland cells producing hydrochloric acid and intrinsic factor.
Gastric gland cells releasing pepsinogen and gastric lipase.
Gastric enteroendocrine cells secreting gastrin.
Gastrointestinal endocrine cells producing somatostatin.
Gastric cells forming a mucus and bicarbonate-rich barrier that protects the stomach lining.
Strong acid secreted by gastric parietal cells that supports protein denaturation and pepsin activation.
Protein secreted by gastric parietal cells required for efficient vitamin B12 absorption in the terminal ileum.
Inactive precursor secreted by chief cells that is converted into pepsin in the acidic stomach.
Protease active at low pH that breaks dietary proteins into shorter peptides.
Fat-digesting enzyme secreted by gastric chief cells.
Protective combination of mucus, bicarbonate, epithelial integrity, and repair limiting damage from gastric acid.
Preparatory gastric response to sight, smell, taste, or thought of food mediated substantially through vagal signals.
Gastric activation triggered by stomach distension and the presence of food, especially peptides.
Regulatory response when chyme enters the duodenum; includes inhibition of gastric secretion and emptying.
Neural and hormonal feedback from the small intestine that slows stomach activity.
Cranial nerve carrying important parasympathetic signals between brainstem and digestive organs.
Reflex in which gastric activity promotes ileal movement and transfer toward the cecum.
Hormone from gastric G cells that generally increases gastric acid secretion and activity.
Hormone released in response to intestinal fat and protein that stimulates pancreatic enzyme secretion and gallbladder contraction.
Intestinal hormone released in response to acidic chyme that promotes bicarbonate-rich pancreatic secretion.
Intestinal K-cell hormone that supports glucose-dependent insulin secretion; also called glucose-dependent insulinotropic polypeptide.
Inhibitory hormone that suppresses gastrin and gastric acid secretion, among other effects.
Enteric neuropeptide that supports intestinal vasodilation and secretion.
Small-intestinal enteroendocrine cells that secrete cholecystokinin.
Duodenal enteroendocrine cells that secrete secretin in response to acid.
Intestinal enteroendocrine cells that secrete GIP.
First segment of the small intestine receiving gastric chyme, bile, and pancreatic secretions.
Middle segment of small intestine where substantial nutrient digestion and absorption occurs.
Distal small-intestinal segment specialized in bile-salt and vitamin B12 uptake, ending at the ileocecal valve.
Permanent circular folds of small-intestinal mucosa and submucosa increasing contact and surface area.
Fingerlike small-intestinal mucosal projections containing absorptive epithelium, capillaries, and lacteals.
Tiny projections of enterocyte apical membranes that form the intestinal brush border.
Microvillus-rich absorptive surface carrying enzymes for terminal digestive steps.
Absorptive epithelial cells lining intestinal villi.
Specialized lymphatic capillaries in intestinal villi that receive dietary lipid particles.
Lipoprotein particles assembled in intestinal cells to transport absorbed long-chain dietary lipids into lymph.
Vein delivering nutrient-rich blood from the GI tract and related organs to the liver.
Submucosal duodenal glands releasing alkaline mucus that helps protect and neutralize the proximal intestine.
Aggregated lymphoid nodules prominent in the ileum that contribute to intestinal immune surveillance.
Intestinal crypt cells that release antimicrobial molecules such as lysozyme and defensins.
Epithelial cells secreting protective mucus in intestines and other mucosal surfaces.
Tubular intestinal gland invaginations between villi that house secretory and renewing cells.
Sphincter-like junction between terminal ileum and cecum regulating passage into the large intestine.
Small aggregates of bile salts and lipid-digestion products that assist lipid delivery to the intestinal brush border.
Terminal-ileal uptake of vitamin B12 bound to intrinsic factor.
Broad part of the pancreas nestled within the C-shaped duodenum.
Elongated central part of pancreas extending behind the stomach.
Narrow end of pancreas extending toward the spleen.
Exocrine cell clusters that produce digestive enzymes for release into ducts.
Endocrine cell clusters releasing hormones such as insulin and glucagon into the blood.
Pancreatic enzyme that breaks down starch and other digestible polysaccharides.
Pancreatic enzyme that hydrolyzes triglycerides during small-intestinal fat digestion.
Protein-digesting enzymes including trypsin, chymotrypsin, elastase, and carboxypeptidases.
Pancreatic enzymes that break down nucleic acids.
Inactive pancreatic precursor of trypsin that is activated in the small intestine.
Duct carrying pancreatic exocrine secretion toward the duodenum.
Additional pancreatic drainage duct that may open at the minor duodenal papilla.
Alkaline ductal secretion that helps neutralize acidic chyme entering the duodenum.
Principal liver cells responsible for metabolism, protein synthesis, and bile production.
Resident macrophages within liver sinusoids that remove particles and help immune surveillance.
Specialized, permeable hepatic blood channels supporting exchange between blood and hepatocytes.
Large right-sided anatomical lobe of the liver.
Left-sided anatomical lobe of the liver.
Liver lobe on the posterior visceral surface near the inferior vena cava.
Liver lobe on the inferior surface near the gallbladder fossa.
Peritoneal fold visible on the anterior liver surface separating right and left anatomical lobes.
Fibrous remnant of the fetal umbilical vein located in the liver's inferior falciform region.
Small organ beneath the liver that stores and concentrates bile.
Liver-produced fluid containing bile salts that assists lipid emulsification but contains no digestive enzymes.
Amphipathic molecules derived from bile acids that emulsify fats and assist micelle formation.
Dispersal of large lipid droplets into smaller droplets, increasing accessible surface area for lipase action.
Recycling of bile salts from intestine, especially terminal ileum, through portal blood back to the liver.
Duct draining bile from the right side of the liver.
Duct draining bile from the left side of the liver.
Duct formed by the convergence of the right and left hepatic ducts.
Duct connecting the gallbladder with the extrahepatic biliary duct system.
Duct formed by union of the common hepatic and cystic ducts, carrying bile toward duodenum.
Common channel where bile and pancreatic secretions often converge before entering the duodenum.
Mucosal projection in descending duodenum where bile and pancreatic secretions commonly enter.
Smooth-muscle complex regulating delivery of bile and pancreatic fluid into the duodenum.
Blind pouch at the beginning of the large intestine receiving contents from the ileum.
Narrow, blind-ended lymphoid-rich extension of the cecum.
Right-sided segment of colon running from cecum toward the hepatic flexure.
Bend between ascending and transverse colon near the liver.
Colon segment extending across the abdomen between right and left colic flexures.
Bend between transverse and descending colon near the spleen.
Left-sided colon segment descending from splenic flexure toward sigmoid colon.
S-shaped segment connecting descending colon to rectum.
Distal large-intestinal chamber storing feces before defecation.
Saclike pouches of the colon formed by muscular tone and its arrangement.
Three longitudinal smooth-muscle bands characteristic of most of the colon.
Small fat-filled tags attached to the outer surface of the colon.
Involuntary smooth-muscle sphincter normally maintaining anal canal closure.
Voluntary skeletal-muscle sphincter supporting conscious control of defecation.
Reflex initiated by rectal stretch that increases rectal contractions and relaxes the internal anal sphincter.
Community of microorganisms in the digestive tract that includes organisms able to ferment otherwise indigestible carbohydrates.
Microbial fermentation products such as acetate, propionate, and butyrate that can be absorbed in the colon.
Backflow of stomach contents into the esophagus that can cause heartburn.
Inflammation of the stomach lining.
Break in the stomach or duodenal mucosal lining associated with acid-peptic injury.
Inflammation of the pancreas, often related to gallstones or alcohol exposure.
Solid deposits formed in the gallbladder or biliary tract that can obstruct bile flow.
Inflammation of the liver, with possible viral and nonviral causes.
Advanced liver scarring and architectural distortion resulting from chronic liver injury.
Yellowing of skin or eyes resulting from elevated bilirubin.
Inflammation of the colon.
Frequent loose or watery stools, often reflecting abnormal secretion, absorption, or transit.
Difficult or infrequent passage of stools, often associated with slow transit or hard stools.
Diarrheal disease caused by toxigenic Vibrio cholerae, producing large intestinal fluid losses.
Inflammation of the gingivae (gums).
Disease affecting supporting structures of teeth, often involving plaque-associated inflammation.
Viral infection that can cause inflammation of salivary glands, especially the parotid glands.
